author: Lukasz Olejnik
text: A critical security flaw found by an Anthropic researcher (using AI) affects wolfSSL, a library used in products from VPN apps and home routers to automotive systems, power grid infrastructure, and military systems. CVE-2026-5194 could let a device or application accept a forged digital identity as genuine, trusting a malicious server, file, or connection it should have rejected. The flaw comes from missing digest-size and OID checks in signature verification, and Red Hat rates it CVSSv3 10.0 (max; remotely exploitable, no privileges required, no user interaction needed).
suggestedEngagement: Connect to the enterprise deployment angle: 'The scarier implication for enterprises is that agents using wolfSSL-based libraries for TLS could silently trust forged certificates from lateral-movement attacks. CVSSv3 10.0 in a dependency you may not even know you ship. What's your threat model for AI agents that inherit cryptographic trust from their host environment?'

Highlight the dual-use irony: 'Fascinating that the same AI pushing enterprises toward agent deployments is also the tool that found this flaw — and wolfSSL shows up in the very embedded infrastructure agents are starting to interact with. Glasswing may be the most underrated security initiative right now.'

Ask about scope awareness: 'The wolfSSL surface area is wild — VPNs, routers, automotive, military. What percentage of enterprises do you think know they ship wolfSSL transitively through their agent toolchains?'

author: Debjani Ghosh
text: 3 key takeaways from the Standford HAI 2026 AI Index Report: Overall take - the 2025 HAI report was about AI becoming mainstream, faster, cheaper, and more useful. Transparency is moving backward: the most powerful models now disclose the least. Transparency Index fell from 58 to 40 in a single year. Talent inflow to the U.S. collapsed 89% since 2017; younger U.S. developers (22-25) saw employment fall nearly 20% in 2024.

author: Zvi Mowshowitz
text: Claude Mythos: The System Card — Claude Mythos is the first model other than GPT-2 not being released for public use at all. If given to anyone with a credit card, Mythos would give attackers a cornucopia of zero-day exploits for essentially all the software on Earth. Notably: cyber was not a major category in RSPv3, despite Anthropic knowing about Mythos at the time RSPv3 was issued. author: Diptanu Choudhury
text: We are seeing backlash against sandboxes for primarily a couple of reasons - vendors don't support users to overcommit compute. You can't pay for N cores and overcommit the number of sandboxes that are run on those cores. In reality agents don't uniformly use resources during [quoting @arlanr: 'Turning the entire web into a filesystem. Code hallucinations are not a model problem. They're a data problem. Every day, APIs ship breaking changes, deprecate endpoints, and rename parameters. Models can't keep up because their training...']
suggestedEngagement: Share the compute scheduling angle from enterprise deployments: 'The overcommit problem is real — we see it with enterprise clients trying to scale agent pools. Burst-friendly pricing (pay per sandbox-second vs. reserved cores) seems like the unlock, but it shifts risk back to the vendor. Is tensorlake working on a scheduler-side solution, or is this a pricing model problem?'

Engage on the data hallucination layer from the @arlanr quote: 'The data-not-model framing is sharp. For enterprise deployments the implication is that API-aware retrieval (live docs, versioned specs) becomes a reliability control, not just a nice-to-have. Does turning the web into a filesystem actually solve the stale-spec problem or just move it?'

Connect both threads: 'The resource overcommit problem and the hallucination problem both point at the same architectural gap — sandboxes need to be cheap enough to run many in parallel, and agents need live context to be reliable.
